flawed_step: Lines 0019-0028 (the inference that S contains factors of 1,2,...,n and the resulting factorization m(m+1)...(m+n-1) = k_1 * 2k_2 * 3k_3 * ... * n k_n)
counterexample: Take m = 5, n = 4, so S = {5, 6, 7, 8} and m^(4 rising) = 5*6*7*8 = 1680. Line 0025 asserts the product of the n elements of S can be written as a product of n factors, the j-th of which is j*k_j; since S has exactly n = 4 elements and the right side has exactly 4 factors, this assigns to each j in {1,2,3,4} a DISTINCT element of S divisible by j. That assignment does not exist here: the only element of S divisible by 3 is 6, the only element divisible by 4 is 8, and the only elements divisible by 2 are 6 and 8. So the three indices j = 2, 3, 4 must all draw from the two-element set {6, 8} (Hall's condition fails: |{6,8}| = 2 < 3), and no such system of distinct representatives exists. Concretely, the lemma cited in lines 0011-0017 yields 5 for j=1, 6 for j=2, 6 again for j=3 (6 is the only multiple of 3 in {5,6,7}), and 8 for j=4 — element 6 is used twice and element 7 is never used, so the elements of S cannot be matched one-to-one with the factors 1,2,3,4 as line 0025 requires. (The theorem's conclusion is still true here, 1680 = 70 * 4!, but the proof's derivation of it fails.)
reasoning_summary: The proof's engine is the step from 'each initial segment {m,...,m+j-1} contains a multiple of j' to 'the product of the n elements of S factors as (k_1)(2k_2)(3k_3)...(n k_n)'. Because S has exactly n elements and the displayed product has exactly n factors, this step silently requires a system of distinct representatives: n distinct elements of S, the j-th divisible by j. The cited lemma gives no distinctness — the same element can be the witness for several j. For m = 5, n = 4 the required SDR provably does not exist: the multiples of 2, 3, 4 inside {5,6,7,8} all lie in {6,8}, so three indices compete for two elements. Hence line 0025's equation is unattainable and line 0028's regrouping into (k_1...k_n) * n! never gets off the ground. The stated theorem is true (it equals the integrality of a binomial coefficient), but this argument does not establish it.
counterexample_target: the factorization claim at line 0025, not the theorem statement
